picked.t: Vietnam seeks broader visa exemptions for high-potential tourism markets
picked.body: Under a draft resolution that the government submitted to the National Assembly on Saturday, visa policies will also be designed with flexibility tailored to specific markets, with priority given to high-spending, long-stay tourists, repeat travelers and those combining leisure trips with business, conferences or seminars. The draft covers seven key policy groups, including investment incentives, business support, nighttime economy development, human resource, visa policies and tourism infrastructure. Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Lam Thi Phuong Thanh said the proposed policies aim to remove existing bottlenecks and attract investment, positioning tourism as a key economic sector and a driver of the country's goal of achieving double-digit economic growth. The National Assembly is expected to vote on adopting the resolution on Nov. 21. Vietnam received 19.5 million international visitors in the first 10 months of 2026, a 13.8% increase from a year earlier, as it eyes 25 million foreign arrivals by the end of this year. China, South Korea and Russia are the country's biggest source of inbound tourists. Vietnam currently grants visa exemptions to citizens of 39 countries, allowing stays from 14 to 90 days.

picked.t: Vietnam eyes 24/7 entertainment zones, tax holidays for billion-dollar tourism projects
picked.body: The draft resolution on special mechanisms and policies for tourism development, submitted to lawmakers on Saturday, sets out seven groups of policies, ranging from investment incentives and business support to the night-time economy, workforce training and infrastructure. Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Lam Thi Phuong Thanh said the policies aim to clear bottlenecks, draw investment and make tourism a key economic sector that helps drive the country's double-digit growth target. Under the draft, incentives would be tiered by investment capital, number of jobs and type of project, and concentrated in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang as well as tourism centers, national tourism areas and areas with national tourism potential. High-quality tourism projects with total investment of at least VND3 trillion, at least VND1.5 trillion of it for tourism components, and creating at least 1,000 jobs could receive infrastructure support inside and outside the project site and priority in promotion. Domestic investors in this tier could also rent unused state-owned houses and land. Catalyst tourism projects worth at least VND10 trillion, with at least VND5 trillion for tourism components and at least 1,500 jobs, would be eligible on a five-year pilot basis for a preferential corporate income tax rate as low as 10%, half Vietnam's standard 20% rate, plus land rent exemptions or reductions set by the government. The highest incentives would go to strategic projects with total investment of at least VND30 trillion, including at least VND15 trillion for tourism components, and at least 2,000 jobs. They could operate for up to 70 years, be exempt from corporate income tax for up to four years and have their tax cut by up to 50% for no more than nine years after that. None of the three tiers would cover casino, prize-winning electronic gaming, betting or real estate components, Thanh said, as incentives would apply only to tourism activities. The government also proposed a pilot cut of up to 30% in land rent for landscaped areas, green space, water surfaces and shared spaces not used directly for business at resort hotels rated four stars or above, provided they are in tourism centers or national tourism areas and have a gross building density below 25%. Businesses opening new air routes for tourism could receive support, as could travel firms and accommodation providers that sign long-term contracts to buy products certified under the One Commune One Product (OCOP) program, which promotes local specialties. For new business models, the draft offers incentives for complexes combining tourism, entertainment, culture and sports; for tourism combined with healthcare and medical treatment; and for activities involving local communities. Businesses would also be encouraged to use artificial intelligence, virtual reality, augmented reality and other new technologies to develop products and improve the visitor experience. Some large-scale performing arts complexes, concert halls, festival streets, integrated entertainment zones and night-time economy activities would be allowed to operate 24/7 under a pilot of up to five years. They could follow shortened administrative procedures and obtain a one-time license for large international art programs and events held regularly, instead of reapplying for each edition. The state budget would fund training for high-quality tourism workers in management, foreign languages, vocational skills, digital transformation, digital content creation and innovation, as well as for local workers in community tourism areas. Budget funding would be prioritized for essential infrastructure and multimodal transport links from international gateways to growth poles, key tourism centers and national tourism areas. The state would also support the national tourism promotion program and help localities develop distinctive products and community tourism in ethnic minority, mountainous, border, island and disadvantaged areas. Reviewing the draft, Nguyen Dac Vinh, chairman of the National Assembly's Committee for Culture and Society, said the committee supported special policies focused on projects able to lead and spread tourism growth in key areas. But the committee found the incentives for strategic catalyst projects had been set at a very high level without an assessment of the benefits they would bring, and asked that they be weighed carefully. It also asked the government to explain how the minimum capital thresholds and the share of capital reserved for tourism were set, and whether the criteria for classifying projects were feasible. The committee said casino, prize-winning electronic gaming, betting and real estate components must stay outside the incentives, and that support should be tied to project results so the policy cannot be used to develop businesses outside priority sectors. picked.t: Vietnam targets at least 10% GDP growth and $6,100 per capita GDP in 2027
picked.body: The legislature passed a resolution on the country's 2027 socio-economic development plan on Saturday, with more than 93.4% of lawmakers voting in favor. Under the resolution, Vietnam aims to achieve economic growth of at least 10% next year while keeping inflation at around 4.5%. The resolution calls on the government to continue prioritizing growth while maintaining macroeconomic stability, controlling inflation and ensuring major economic balances. The government is also tasked with making breakthroughs in mobilizing and efficiently allocating resources for development. Measures include increasing state budget revenue, cutting expenditure, particularly recurrent spending, issuing various types of bonds and securing official development assistance (ODA) loans. It must also promptly implement policies to raise foreign ownership limits in industries and sectors that do not affect national security. The National Assembly urged the government to manage interest and exchange rates in line with domestic and international conditions, lower lending rates and direct credit toward production, business activities and priority sectors. The government is also expected to introduce effective measures to address trade deficit, develop a healthy and sustainable real estate market, and resolve long-standing stalled projects. To ensure energy security, the resolution requires the government to guarantee sufficient supplies of electricity and petroleum products under all circumstances. On infrastructure, the government is tasked with completing the expressway network in line with approved plans, particularly the eastern and western sections of the North-South Expressway and East-West transport corridors. It must also accelerate major national railway projects, including the Lao Cai-Hanoi-Hai Phong railway, the North-South high-speed railway, international rail connections and urban railway networks. The resolution calls for faster progress on two major airport projects: Long Thanh International Airport in Dong Nai, about 40 kilometers east of Ho Chi Minh City, and Gia Binh International Airport in Bac Ninh Province, 40 km east of central Hanoi. Long Thanh is being developed to ease pressure on HCMC's Tan Son Nhat International Airport and eventually handle 100 million passengers annually. Gia Binh is planned as a major aviation gateway for northern Vietnam, serving passenger and cargo transport, international transit and aircraft maintenance. In the energy sector, the National Assembly requires the government to develop a national energy reserve strategy and accelerate planned power generation, transmission grid and solar power projects. It also urged authorities to firmly address the trend of localities pursuing airport, seaport, data center and free trade zone investments without proper planning, warning against wasteful spending.

picked.t: Steak, pizza, and French food: 8 European restaurants to try in Hanoi
picked.body: Chien Beo Steak After remaining closed for nearly a decade, Chien Beo Steak reopened in mid-2025. It had once been a popular destination for generations of Hanoian families. Its standout dishes include cheese-wrapped beef rolls and steak, made in a style adapted to Vietnamese palates. The restaurant's seating area is now cleaner and more spacious than before. Tables can be hard to book since they are often full. Chien Beo only serves dinner and is closed on Mondays. Address: 69 Hoang Nhu Tiep Street, Long Bien Ward. Prices start at VND250,000 ($9.60) per person. Pizza 4P's chain Pizza 4P's, a Japanese Italian pizza chain, offers a range of pizzas with thin crusts alongside pasta, salads, and desserts. It is good for families with children and groups of friends. Its spaces are dotted with greenery, and diners can watch the chefs at work. Address: Bao Khanh Street, Trang Tien Street, Au Co Street, Lotte Center, and Hanoi Center. Prices start at VND300,000 ($11.50) per person. La Bodega La Bodega spreads across a space of 2,500 square meters at a location quite far from the city center. The menu features Italian and European staples like pizza, pasta, and grilled meats. A standout dish to try is the Picanha BBQ, a top sirloin cap beef cut. The restaurant seats 200 guests and often hosts gatherings of friends, family parties, and small events. Address: Alley 56/139 Thach Cau, Long Bien Ward. Prices start at VND300,000 per person. Caffè Italia (Casa Italia) Set in Hanoi's Italian Cultural Center (Casa Italia), the restaurant features a spacious Mediterranean garden perfect for outdoor dining and wine. The menu includes Italian classics like pizza, pasta, and gelato. The restaurant also has a board on which it lists dishes outside the regular menu, which changes frequently. Address: 18 Le Phung Hieu Street, Hoan Kiem Ward. Prices range from VND300,000 to VND500,000 per person. Mediterraneo Mediterraneo stands out for its setting. Some tables offer a view of St. Joseph's Cathedral. It is a good choice for people looking to try Italian cuisine beyond just pizza and pasta. Tripadvisor recommends Mediterraneo among Italian restaurants to try in Hanoi, and it won a Travelers' Choice award in 2025. Address: 23 Nha Tho Street, Hoan Kiem Ward. Prices range from VND500,000 to VND700,000 per person, not including alcoholic drinks. Cugini Cugini positions itself as a bistro focused on modern Italian cuisine. Its appeal lies in the balance it strikes between food quality and atmosphere. The restaurant has an outdoor seating area and a second floor. Cugini is more affordable than Hanoi's high-end Italian restaurants, and comes recommended by Tripadvisor. Address: 67 To Ngoc Van Street, Tay Ho Ward. Prices start at around VND400,000 per person, not including alcoholic drinks. Colette French Bistro & Wine Bar Colette is compact and in French bistro style. The menu centers on French dishes such as tuna tartare, beef braised in wine, and foie gras. Its location in the Old Quarter is also an advantage for those looking to pair dinner with exploring central Hanoi. Address: 12 Lo Su Street, Hoan Kiem Ward. Prices are around VND500,000 per person, not including alcoholic drinks. Samé - bistrot & wine Samé follows a French bistro style with a Vietnamese touch, and has 30 covers. It uses Vietnamese ingredients, which sets it apart from other French restaurants in the city. Popular dishes include beef carpaccio, whole fried quail with smoked sriracha sauce, and light bites such as paprika fries. Address: 29 Le Thanh Tong Street, Cua Nam Ward. Prices are around VND500,000 per person, not including alcoholic drinks.

picked.t: Two Ho Chi Minh City students win iPhone 17s for frequent bus travel
picked.body: The awards were presented Friday by the Ho Chi Minh City Public Transport Management Center, based on data from its payment and identification system. The center identified 10 students with the highest number of valid bus trips between Oct. 1 and 15. Tran Thanh Luong, a student at the University of Transport in Ho Chi Minh City, topped the ranking and received an iPhone 17 with 256 GB of storage. The other nine students were selected through a lucky draw. Le Quy, a student at the College of Radio and Television II, won the second iPhone 17 256 GB, provided by another sponsor. The remaining students received shopping vouchers worth VND1-2 million each. "I’ve taken the bus about 200 to 300 times (over Oct. 1-15)," Luong said. He regularly travels by bus to university and his part-time job. He also uses the journeys to observe transport management and operations, the field he is studying. "I never imagined that riding the bus could lead to winning an iPhone," Quy said, adding that buses are a convenient way for students to get around. Le Hoan, deputy director of the center, said this was the first time it had organized such a program. The initiative aims to encourage students and young people to use public buses and help ease traffic congestion. The center plans to continue it. Ho Chi Minh City has offered free rides on 134 public bus routes since July 1. These routes have carried more than 40 million passengers since, nearly 50% more than during the same period last year.

picked.t: South Korean low-cost airlines slash Southeast Asia fares as tourists favor Japan, China
picked.body: Jeju Air is offering discounts of up to 77% on February flights from Incheon and Busan to Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and the Philippines, ChosunBiz reported. Trinity Airways, formerly T'way Air, is cutting Southeast Asian fares by 22% for travel through January. A Jeju Air flight from Incheon to Da Nang on Nov. 21 has base fares starting at just 10,000 won, while Trinity Airways listed an Incheon-Nha Trang flight on Nov. 1 for 15,000 won. However, fuel surcharges and airport fees can add 110,000-190,000 won each way, with extra baggage and meals potentially costing further. Airlines are lowering fares to fill seats on flights they need to maintain to retain operating rights and airport slots. Selling cheap tickets helps cover some costs, even if the flights remain unprofitable, industry officials told ChosunBiz . Routes between Incheon and Vietnam carried 7.33 million passengers in the first nine months of the year, down 5.4% from a year earlier, according to Air Transportation Information Portal data. Passenger numbers on the Thailand and Philippines routes fell by 14% each. On the other hand, passenger traffic between South Korea and Japan rose by 20.3% in the first eight months, while China routes recorded a 23% increase, Seoul Economic Daily reported, citing transport ministry data. The newspaper said a weak yen had helped attract travelers to Japan, and new flight connections had made China more accessible. Shorter flights also mean lower fuel surcharges than trips to Southeast Asia. Alongside fare cuts, Trinity Airways plans to suspend certain flights to Da Nang, Nha Trang, and Bangkok during the winter schedule to limit losses.

picked.t: Vietnam's top leader begins official visit to Japan
picked.body: During the visit, the Vietnamese leader is expected to meet Japan's Emperor and Empress, Prime Minister, and the presidents of both houses of parliament. He will also meet leaders of economic organizations and major corporations, attend and deliver a speech at the Vietnam-Japan Public-Private Forum on Economic and Science-Technology Cooperation, and visit a high-tech enterprise. The Vietnamese delegation includes Politburo members and Party Central Committee secretaries Nguyen Duy Ngoc, chairman of the Party Central Committee's Commission for Organization, and Le Minh Tri, chairman of the Commission for Internal Affairs. Other Politburo members joining the trip are General Phan Van Giang, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense; General Luong Tam Quang, Minister of Public Security; Le Hoai Trung, Minister of Foreign Affairs; Tran Duc Thang, Secretary of the Hanoi Party Committee; and Tran Luu Quang, Secretary of the Ho Chi Minh City Party Committee. The delegation also comprises Party Central Committee Members Nguyen Hai Ninh, Chief of the Party Central Committee Office; Ngo Van Tuan, Minister of Finance; Le Manh Hung, Minister of Industry and Trade; Vu Hai Quan, Minister of Science and Technology; and Trinh Viet Hung, Minister of Agriculture and Environment. Deputy Foreign Minister Nguyen Minh Vu said the visit holds strategic significance in three key areas. First, the two nations will establish an overarching strategic vision for bilateral relations in a new era, with leaders jointly identifying long-term cooperation priorities across various sectors to meet mutual development needs. Second, Vietnam and Japan will move beyond conventional economic, trade, and investment cooperation toward deeper economic integration. This shift will place greater emphasis on partnership, co-creation, and strengthening each country's economic autonomy and resilience. Third, the visit will provide momentum for breakthroughs in science, technology, innovation, and the transformation of development models. Japan brings strengths in advanced technology, capital, management experience, and manufacturing, while Vietnam offers a young workforce, a dynamic market, significant growth potential, and a strong commitment to promoting innovation. Vietnam and Japan established diplomatic relations in 1973 and upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2023. Japan is currently Vietnam's largest provider of official development assistance (ODA), its top labor cooperation partner, third-largest investor, and fourth-largest tourism and trading partner. Bilateral trade reached US$43.7 billion in the first nine months this year, up 15% year-on-year. Trade turnover had reached $51.43 billion in 2025. The Vietnamese community in Japan numbers nearly 700,000, featuring a growing proportion of intellectuals and highly skilled professionals. Currently, around 7,000 Vietnamese IT engineers are working in the country.

picked.t: American-style dining in Ho Chi Minh City skyscraper
picked.body: Opened in late September, the restaurant is the first Asian location for the American steakhouse chain founded in 1990. Spanning around 500 m2 and with 120 covers, the restaurant operates as an authentic American steakhouse. Stanley Ko, president of Ko Hospitality Group, the operator of The Capital Grille in Vietnam, says Ho Chi Minh City was selected as the brand's first regional destination due to its dynamic economy, sizable business community, and diners who are open to western foods. The restaurant serves an à la carte menu featuring appetizers, soups, salads, beef, seafood, side dishes, and desserts, with portion sizes adjusted to suit local dining habits. Beef takes center stage with diverse options in cuts, portion weights, levels of doneness, and sauces. The eatery exclusively serves imported USDA Prime beef, the highest grade in the U.S. Department of Agriculture quality system, known for abundant marbling that enhances tenderness and flavor when cooked. The restaurant's signature offering is its dry-aged beef (pictured). Aged for 18 to 24 days in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room, the process reduces moisture content, tenderizes muscle fibers, and deepens the natural flavor profile. A 680-gram dry-aged steak portion, good for three to four diners, costs VND3.2 million (US$124). The menu also highlights recognizable American classics. The caviar dip, priced at VND1.9 million, offers a twist on standard "chips and dip" by pairing crispy potato chips with caviar and caramelized onion dip. The lobster bisque, priced at VND450,000 per portion, is a steakhouse staple rooted in French tradition. It features a velvety crustacean-based broth combined with cream and seasonings, served alongside Spanish sherry, an aged fortified wine that elevates the soup's aroma and depth of flavor. Meanwhile, the lobster mac and cheese, priced at VND800,000, features macaroni tossed in cheese sauce and mixed with lobster meat. This is a variation of "mac and cheese," an iconic dish introduced to formal American banquets by President Thomas Jefferson in the early 19th century before becoming a household staple following Kraft's boxed release in 1937. Shannon Dean and Michael Zack, tourists from the U.S. visiting HCMC in late October, dined at the restaurant to enjoy some familiar flavors after trying local dishes. Having visited The Capital Grille in Las Vegas before, both said the food and decor closely matched U.S. standards, creating a sense of familiarity. For them, the highlight was pairing a familiar meal with panoramic city views at prices similar to the brand's U.S. locations. Local diners have also shared their impressions. A family of four from Ho Chi Minh City visited the restaurant to experience high-floor dining in the city center. Ordering a 10-course meal across appetizers, soups, steaks, seafood, and desserts, they observed that the dishes featured large portions, rich and creamy flavors, and fewer green vegetable options, with some items feeling slightly dry for Vietnamese palates. Their meal cost nearly VND13 million, which was similar to prices at other high-end steakhouses in the city. A staff member sets the table before welcoming dinner guests to the restaurant, which charges a 5% service charge. The restaurant is open from 11:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. and from 5:30 p.m. to 9:30 p.m. Guests are required to make reservations in advance and can use a dedicated elevator and private entrance (pictured).
